lesson.title: One Path, One Current: How Series Circuits Behave
lesson.summary: Defines a series circuit as components connected end to end along a single current path, shows why current is identical everywhere in that loop, and works through resistor voltage drops using Ohm's law.
lesson.body:
A series circuit is the simplest possible arrangement of multiple components: they are connected end to end, one after another, forming a single loop with exactly one path for current to travel. Because charge has nowhere else to go and cannot pile up anywhere inside a wire under steady conditions, the current at every single point around that loop must be identical, whether you measure it right at the source, between the first and second resistor, or anywhere else along the path. This is a direct consequence of charge conservation, the same principle you have already seen underlying current itself.

While current stays the same throughout a series loop, voltage does not. Each resistor in the path uses Ohm's law, V = IR, to determine its own individual voltage drop based on that shared current and its own particular resistance value. Since the resistors have different resistance values in general, they produce different voltage drops, even though the exact same current flows through each of them. The sum of all these individual drops around the loop must equal the total voltage supplied by the source, a balance that later coursework formalizes as Kirchhoff's voltage law.

Consider three resistors, 100 ohms, 220 ohms, and 470 ohms, connected in series across a 9 volt battery. Resistors in series simply add, so the total resistance is R_total = 100 + 220 + 470 = 790 ohms. By Ohm's law, the single current flowing through this entire loop is I = V / R_total = 9 / 790, which is approximately 0.0114 amps, or 11.4 milliamps. That same 11.4 milliamps flows through all three resistors. The individual voltage drops follow from V = IR for each: about 1.14 volts across the 100 ohm resistor, 2.51 volts across the 220 ohm resistor, and 5.35 volts across the 470 ohm resistor. Adding those three drops, 1.14 plus 2.51 plus 5.35, gives approximately 9.0 volts, matching the source, exactly as expected.

This behavior gives series circuits their defining practical characteristic and their defining practical weakness at the same time. Because there is only one path, if any single component in the loop fails open, such as a burnt out filament or a broken wire, current stops flowing everywhere in the loop simultaneously, which is why old style holiday lights wired in series would go completely dark from a single failed bulb. Series wiring also means adding more resistors always increases total resistance and therefore decreases the shared current, since R_total grows with every additional element.

Series resistor combinations are also the foundation for the voltage divider circuit, covered in an upcoming section, which deliberately exploits the fact that different resistors in a series chain drop different, predictable fractions of the source voltage. Recognizing a series connection on sight, one path, shared current, is the first and most important skill for analyzing any circuit that combines series and parallel sections together.
